messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Daniel was 60 and had spent most of his adult life working in warehouses, moving stock, keeping to routines, and doing his best to stay practical. He was in a long-term relationship and, by the time he came for help, his partner had begun to notice how much of the world Daniel now worked to keep at a distance. He had served in the military years earlier, and the event that still sat at the center of his distress was an operation in which others were killed and he survived. When he spoke about it, he could give only fragments, stopping and starting as though the account itself ran into a wall. He would say that he knew what happened, but that he could not find the words to describe it properly. In session, this came across as more than reluctance: there was a sense that language failed him when he tried to put the scene into sequence, as if the experience remained too large, too exact, and too awful to shape into a story.

What Daniel could say was that remembering it did not feel remote or historical. It brought the same terror back into his body. When he was pressed, his face tightened and he became visibly unsettled, as though he had been carried back to the moment rather than merely recalling it. He described the memory as having an immediate force, not like thinking about something that happened years ago but like being returned to the danger itself. Alongside that terror came intense guilt. He was haunted by the fact that he was the one who got out while others did not. He spoke of this with a flatness that seemed brittle rather than detached, and beneath it there was a painful conviction that he had somehow not earned his survival. The memory did not simply bring sadness or regret; it brought a sharp, self-directed blame that left him feeling marked by what had happened.

In the years after the military event, Daniel gradually organized his life around keeping anything that resembled it out of reach. He avoided going to or near the place where it happened, even if that meant taking longer routes or turning down situations that might have brought him close to that area. He also avoided thinking about it, which meant actively pushing away any thought, image, or conversation that might lead him back there. He did this so consistently that his partner had learned not to ask too much, because even a brief question could leave him visibly tense and abruptly silent. Daniel also avoided wearing similar clothes to those he associated with the time of the event. In his ordinary life this showed up in small, deliberate choices: what he would and would not put on in the morning, what he would leave hanging in the closet, and how uneasy he felt when work required anything that reminded him of his military clothing. At the warehouse, where he moved among uniforms, work gear, and the practical clothing of other men on shift, he became increasingly careful about anything that resembled what he once wore. Even if no one else would have noticed, he did, and he would change or layer clothing to keep the resemblance at bay.

Over time, these efforts narrowed his life in ways that had become impossible to ignore. He was still going to work, but his partner described how he had become more restricted in the places he was willing to go outside of it. Daniel himself said that the world now felt dangerous. This was not an abstract belief for him; it was a conclusion he lived with as if it were common sense. Once he had survived something in which others had not, ordinary life no longer felt reliably safe. He moved through his days with the sense that danger could be waiting anywhere, especially where there was even a faint resemblance to the past. At home he seemed different to himself as well. He said he felt like he did not know himself anymore, a statement he gave with visible unease, as though the person who had once gone through life with a clearer sense of who he was had been altered beyond easy recognition.

By the time he sought help, Daniel had reached a point where the effort of keeping the event out of mind and out of sight had become harder to sustain. His partner had urged him after seeing how strongly he reacted when something reminded him of the military years, and after noticing how he avoided whole stretches of the city and certain kinds of clothing without always being able to explain why. Daniel came in wanting relief from the way the memory still gripped him and from the guilt that returned whenever it did. He was not asking to forget what happened so much as to be able to remember it without being thrown back into terror and self-reproach. What he seemed most afraid of was that he would remain trapped in the same rigid sense of danger and estrangement from himself. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was the chance to live more freely without being pulled away from the people and places of his present life by the weight of what had happened long ago.
